newsitem.title: FRANCE: "Lebanon is not a free country" - Patriarch Sfeir.
newsitem.headline: "Lebanon is not a free country" - Patriarch Sfeir.

text.p: Lebanese Christian Maronite Patriarch Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, speaking before Pope John Paul's historic first visit to Beirut, was quoted on Friday as saying Lebanon was not a free country.

And exiled ex-general Michel Aoun said the Pope's visit would be negative as he would insist on peaceful coexistence between Christians and Moslems while ignoring what Aoun called Lebanon's real problems -- Syrian "colonisation" and Israeli occupation in the south.
Sfeir told the French daily Le Monde that elections were held under Syrian control and Christians felt they were not represented in government or parliament.
"Lebanon is not a free country...It has neither sovereignty nor independence. Part of its people have been shunted aside," he said.

The Maronite church, led by Sfeir, has become the main postwar spokesman for many Christians and some Moslems who are bitter at the presence of Syrian forces and the perceived surrender of decision-making powers to Damascus.

Aoun, who was forced into exile in France in 1990 after heading the Christian-led army in an unsuccessful effort to oust the estimated 35,000 Syrian troops from Lebanon, said he feared the Pope would distract attention from the real problems.

"Lebanon suffers a double occupation, by Israel in the south and colonisation by Syrians. Since neither will be mentioned, the visit will throw a veil over the Lebanese problem," he told French television LCI.
"I am not in favour of the visit, although I call upon all Lebanese to warmly greet him," he said.
Pope John Paul's visit, his first to the Middle East in his much-travelled papacy, aims to help Lebanon's Christian minority s to find a role in the country's postwar life.
The Christians emerged defeated and divided from the 1975-90 civil war and have largely refused to reconcile themselves to the Syrian-dominated government.

Sfeir said it was wrong to believe the papal visit, starting on Saturday, would either put a stamp of approval "on the (Syrian) occupation of our country...or, on the contrary, allow a radical change."

"The Pope is not coming to Lebanon to delve into politics but to recall a number of values which the Christians are very attached to: the right to self-determination, the right of the country to independence and sovereignty, the right of equality for all before the law and respect for justice," he said.
Sfeir said he hoped the visit would help to preserve peaceful ties between Christians and Moslems and Lebanon's role as a link between East and West and Islam and Christianity.
